Amazon

Efficient Clustering with Provable Guardrails
for LLM Inference at Scale

Longshaokan Wang Email: longsha@amazon.com    Wai Tsang Keung Email: wkeung@amazon.com    Punit Ghodasara Email: ghopunit@amazon.com    Roman Wang Email: wangrz@amazon.com    Ali Dashti Email: dashtia@amazon.com    Francesc Moreno-Noguer Email: cescmore@amazon.es Affiliation: 
Abstract

Scaling LLM-based applications to millions of users is bottlenecked by the inference cost and latency of modern foundation models. A natural fix is to cluster the inputs and call the LLM only on cluster representatives, letting other members inherit the output — but this is only safe if each member is measurably close to its representative. Existing clustering methods do not offer such per-sample quality control at scale: none jointly guarantee a minimal within-cluster similarity, exact matching of categorical attributes, and scalability to tens of millions of samples. We propose a two-stage algorithm that generates initial clusters with Mini-batch K-Means, then greedily selects representatives within each initial cluster — a step equivalent to the Johnson–Chvátal heuristic for Set Cover over α\alpha-balls in embedding space. The algorithm enforces the similarity and attribute guardrails exactly by construction; and runs in O⁡(n​d+n2​d/K)O(nd+n^{2}d/K) time and O⁡(n​d+n2/K2)O(nd+n^{2}/K^{2}) memory for nn samples, feature dimension dd, and KK initial clusters — linear in nn when KK grows proportionally with nn. We provide benchmarks against common clustering methods on internal and public datasets — our method not only delivers per-sample guardrails but also runs 1010–1000×1000\times faster and scales to data sizes where most standard methods become intractable. Deployed on 38 million customers for a persona-based recommender, the clustering method cut downstream cost and latency by 50-fold while preserving personalization and unblocked the production launch.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in eCommerce applications (Li et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2022; Herold et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2024; Kojima et al., 2022), but their inference cost and latency scale poorly to user bases of tens of millions (Bommasani et al., 2022; Erdil, 2025; Samsi et al., 2023; Pope et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Kwon et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025). A natural way to reduce this cost is to cluster inputs and invoke the downstream LLM only on cluster representatives, at the price of approximation error: all members of a cluster inherit the output computed for the representative. For customer-facing applications, this error must be explicitly controlled—irrelevant recommendations damage trust and, in the worst case, pose safety concerns (e.g., choking-hazard toys surfaced to households with young children).

We consider a production personalized-recommendation pipeline (Figure 1) in which customer shopping personas are mapped to personalized queries via an LLM, products are retrieved, and an LLM-based Marketing Critic filters results. For 3838M customers, the LLM stages alone cost $1.13M and 508 days of wall-clock time under our allocated throughput. Clustering the input personas before the pipeline is therefore essential, but must satisfy four requirements jointly:

  1. 1.

    semantic similarity between each sample and its cluster representative exceeds a user-specified threshold α\alpha as a quality guardrail;

  2. 2.

    all samples in a cluster share identical user-specified categorical attributes (e.g., household composition) as another quality guardrail;

  3. 3.

    the number of clusters is substantially smaller than the initial sample size nn (target ≥10×\geq 10\times reduction) for downstream computation reduction;

  4. 4.

    clustering runtime, memory, and cost scale to n∼107n\sim 10^{7} and remain small relative to the downstream LLM cost saved.

To our knowledge no existing clustering method satisfies all four jointly. We propose a two-stage clustering algorithm that satisfies all four desired requirements: Stage (i) Mini-batch K-Means (Sculley, 2010) produces initial clusters, and (ii) within each initial cluster we iteratively select the point covering the largest number of remaining samples in its α\alpha-ball under the match relation (similarity ≥α\geq\alpha and attribute equality). Stage 2 is exactly the Johnson–Chvátal greedy heuristic for Set Cover restricted to each initial partition, which yields an exact guardrail guarantee and a provable (1+ln⁡|Ck|)(1+\ln|C_{k}|)-approximation on cluster count per initial cluster CkC_{k}. The resulting cluster-size distribution is heavily skewed by design, enabling aggressive tail-trimming for additional data reduction.

Contributions. (1) A simple two-stage clustering algorithm with exact similarity and attribute guardrails, and a set-cover approximation bound on data-reduction efficiency (Appendix D). (2) Complexity analysis showing O⁡(n​d+n2​d/K)O(nd+n^{2}d/K) time and O⁡(n​d+n2/K2)O(nd+n^{2}/K^{2}) memory, linear in nn when K=Θ⁡(n)K=\Theta(n) (Appendix E). (3) Benchmarks against six standard clustering methods on internal and public data showing 10×10\times–1000×1000\times speedups at matched cluster counts (Section 4). (4) A production deployment clustering 38M customers for a 50-fold reduction in downstream compute (Section 5).

2 Related Work

Standard clustering methods (K-Means (MacQueen, 1967), Gaussian Mixture (Dempster et al., 1977), BIRCH (Zhang et al., 1996), Spectral (Shi and Malik, 2000; von Luxburg, 2007)) do not accept minimal-similarity or attribute-equality constraints out of the box. Threshold-based methods such as Community Detection (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), Star Clustering (Aslam et al., 1998), and SimClus Al Hasan et al. (2011) support a similarity threshold but require O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) pairwise computation and do not scale to n∼107n\sim 10^{7}. Lexical near-deduplication (MinHash (Broder, 1997)) cannot handle paraphrases. Closest to our work is SemDedup (Abbas et al., 2023), which uses a two-stage embedding-plus-clustering design for data-efficient pretraining; we differ in (i) enforcing attribute-equality jointly with similarity; and (ii) using greedy set-cover representative selection with a reassignment step, which improves average within-cluster similarity (Table 1) and produces the skewed cluster-size distribution exploited for tail-trimming (Appendix F.1).

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

Let 𝒟={(Pi,𝐀i)}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(P_{i},\mathbf{A}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} with textual content PiP_{i} and categorical attributes 𝐀i\mathbf{A}_{i}. An embedding model fembf_{\text{emb}} maps Pi↦𝐄i∈ℝdP_{i}\mapsto\mathbf{E}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and fsimf_{\text{sim}} denotes cosine similarity. We seek a cluster assignment f^cluster:𝒟→{1,…,n}\widehat{f}_{\text{cluster}}:\mathcal{D}\to\{1,\ldots,n\} whose image is the set of representative indices, subject to the guardrail property

f^cluster​(Pi,𝐀i)=j⟹fsim​(𝐄i,𝐄j)≥α​ and ​𝐀i=𝐀j.\widehat{f}_{\text{cluster}}(P_{i},\mathbf{A}_{i})=j\;\Longrightarrow\;f_{\text{sim}}(\mathbf{E}_{i},\mathbf{E}_{j})\geq\alpha\;\text{ and }\;\mathbf{A}_{i}=\mathbf{A}_{j}. (1)

Equivalently, defining the match relation i∼αj⇔fsim(𝐄i,𝐄j)≥α∧𝐀i=𝐀ji\sim_{\alpha}j\iff f_{\text{sim}}(\mathbf{E}_{i},\mathbf{E}_{j})\geq\alpha\land\mathbf{A}_{i}=\mathbf{A}_{j} and its α\alpha-ball ℬα(i)={j:i∼αj}\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i)=\{j:i\sim_{\alpha}j\}, every sample must be assigned to a representative whose α\alpha-ball covers it. Note ∼α\sim_{\alpha} is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive, which is what makes the problem non-trivial. The formulation extends to any feature vector and any similarity/distance function.

3.2 Two-Stage Algorithm

Algorithm 3.2 proceeds in two stages. Stage 1 runs Mini-batch K-Means on {𝐄i}\{\mathbf{E}_{i}\} to produce KK initial clusters {Ck}\{C_{k}\}. Stage 2 operates independently within each CkC_{k}: it computes the pairwise similarity matrix Si​jS_{ij} and match matrix Mi​j=𝕀{Si​j≥α∧𝐀i=𝐀j}M_{ij}=\mathbb{I}\{S_{ij}\geq\alpha\land\mathbf{A}_{i}=\mathbf{A}_{j}\}, then iteratively selects the point r∗r^{*} with the largest number of still-unmatched matches, designates it a representative, and assigns all its matched points to it. The process repeats until every point is covered. Figure 2 (Appendix) illustrates the procedure on a toy example.

Set-cover view and guarantees. Within each CkC_{k}, Stage 2 is exactly the Johnson–Chvátal greedy heuristic for Set Cover over the candidate family {ℬα​(i)∩Ck:i∈Ck}\{\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i)\cap C_{k}:i\in C_{k}\}. Reflexivity of ∼α\sim_{\alpha} ensures a valid cover always exists. We prove in Appendix D that Algorithm 3.2 satisfies the guardrail (1) exactly, and that the number of selected representatives within each initial cluster obeys |ℛk|≤OPTk⋅(1+ln⁡|Ck|)|\mathcal{R}_{k}|\leq\mathrm{OPT}_{k}\cdot(1+\ln|C_{k}|). Because greedy set-cover prioritizes the largest uncovered set at each step, the resulting cluster-size distribution is heavily right-skewed—an intended feature that enables tail-cluster trimming for further data reduction (Appendix F.1).

Complexity. Stage 1 is O⁡(T1​b​K​d)O(T_{1}bKd) time and O⁡(n​d)O(nd) memory. Stage 2 is O⁡(d​∑knk2)O(d\sum_{k}n_{k}^{2}) time and O⁡(maxk⁡nk2)O(\max_{k}n_{k}^{2}) memory when processed one initial cluster at a time. For balanced nk≈n/Kn_{k}\approx n/K, total complexity is O⁡(n​d+n2​d/K)O(nd+n^{2}d/K) time and O⁡(n​d+n2/K2)O(nd+n^{2}/K^{2}) memory—linear in nn when K=Θ⁡(n)K=\Theta(n). Appendix E shows the full derivation and comparison. The role of KK is a scalability knob: larger KK reduces per-cluster quadratic cost but introduces partition noise that mildly inflates |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| (Table 3).

Optional reassignment. Greedy selection is order-dependent: a point may be covered early by a representative less similar than one chosen later. A post-hoc reassignment step (Algorithm C, Appendix) reassigns each point to its most-similar feasible representative, strictly increasing average within-cluster similarity while preserving |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| and the guardrail (1) (Appendix D). The trade-off is a flatter cluster-size distribution, which slightly reduces tail-trimming efficiency (Appendix F.1).

4 Experiments

We benchmark on 100K-sample subsets of (i) internal customer shopping personas, (ii) AG News (Del Corso et al., 2005; Gulli, 2005), and (iii) Cosmopedia (Ben Allal et al., 2024). The 100K size is chosen because several baselines (Agglomerative, Spectral) become intractable beyond this size. Full setup in Appendix G.

4.1 Within-Cluster Similarity and Runtime

To compare fairly against baselines that do not accept an α\alpha constraint, we fix the number of clusters: we first run our algorithm with α\alpha chosen to yield ∼50×\sim 50\times data reduction (thresholds 0.750.75/0.30.3/0.40.4 for the three datasets), then run each baseline with the matching cluster count. Table 1 reports the average and minimum within-cluster similarity, fraction of samples below α\alpha, and runtime on a single r7i.12xlarge without parallelization.

Two observations: (i) every baseline violates the guardrail on a non-trivial fraction of samples (Min. Sim. well below α\alpha), while our method holds it exactly; (ii) our method is 10×10\times–1000×1000\times faster because the O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) similarity computation is restricted to within each initial cluster of size ≈n/K\approx n/K, not to the full dataset. Notably, running Mini-batch K-Means alone to produce all final clusters is >10×>10\times slower than our two-stage approach at the same cluster count, since running K-Means with K=|ℛ|K=|\mathcal{R}| is dominated by centroid updates across many clusters.

4.2 Cluster-Size Skew and Tail Trimming

The set-cover greedy selects the largest uncovered set first, producing a heavily right-skewed cluster-size distribution (Figure 3, Appendix F). This is a practical advantage: the top 4%4\% of clusters on the internal data cover 90%90\% of customers, so trimming the tail yields an additional 25×25\times data reduction at the cost of dropping a small fraction of users (who can be compensated for by oversampling upstream). Baselines, which target balanced clusters, achieve at most ∼30%\sim 30\% coverage at the same 4%4\% threshold. The reassignment variant (Section 3.2) partially flattens this distribution, trading tail-trimming efficiency for higher average similarity.

4.3 Similarity as a Proxy for Recommendation Relevance

The guardrail (1) is only useful if within-cluster similarity correlates with downstream recommendation relevance. We stratified-sample 7,000 member–representative pairs across 7 similarity buckets (0.20.2–0.90.9), generate 15 recommendations per representative, and have an LLM-based Marketing Critic rate each (member, product) pair on a 1–5 relevance scale. The Pearson/Spearman correlations between pair similarity and mean relevance are 0.7810.781/0.7970.797 (p<0.001p<0.001; scatter in Figure 5, Appendix), empirically validating embedding similarity as a proxy for recommendation relevance.

5 Production Deployment

We deployed Algorithm 3.2 in a June 2025 A/B test of the recommendation pipeline in Figure 1, targeting 38M customers with α=0.77\alpha=0.77 and exact matching on adult gender, adult count, child presence, child gender, and child age. The threshold α=0.77\alpha=0.77 was chosen via offline validation to balance recommendation relevance against the throughput ceiling imposed by our allocated LLM budget; the attribute-matching constraints reflect product-safety considerations (e.g., age-appropriateness) not captured by embedding similarity alone. Clustering achieves ∼\sim50×50\times data reduction, shrinking the LLM query-generation step from $114,000/22.8 days (cost/time) to $2,100/0.4 days and the Marketing Critic step from $1,018,500/485 days to $20,370/9.7 days—an aggregate ∼\sim50-fold reduction in downstream LLM compute and wall-clock time.

To validate that clustering preserves recommendation quality at scale, we applied the Marketing Critic to 5,000 representative–member pairs: the product-to-member relevance rate is only 0.7%0.7\% below the product-to-representative rate, confirming that the α\alpha-guardrail translates to minimal end-quality loss. This gap is small relative to the ∼\sim50×50\times compute and latency savings downstream. The A/B test showed statistically significant positive impact on business metrics and enabled subsequent launches built on the same clustering infrastructure.

6 Conclusion

We presented a two-stage clustering algorithm that reframes the LLM-inference-scaling problem as greedy set cover over α\alpha-balls in embedding space, yielding exact within-cluster similarity and attribute guardrails, a (1+ln⁡|Ck|)(1+\ln|C_{k}|) approximation on cluster count, and linear-in-nn runtime for K=Θ⁡(n)K=\Theta(n). Empirically it is 1010–1000×1000\times faster than standard baselines at matched cluster counts, and in production it enabled a 50-fold downstream computation reduction for a 38M-customer recommender system. Future directions include richer similarity metrics that better predict LLM output agreement, and learned representatives that minimize cluster count under the guardrail.

Appendix A Design Considerations and Technical Details

By design, the algorithm proposed in Section 3.2 satisfies all the desired requirements listed in Section 1: Steps 4-5 ensure that any customer and their matched representative customer will have a persona similarity above the user-specified threshold and share the same user-specified attributes. The initial clustering allows the more expensive pairwise similarity computation to be performed within an initial cluster instead of for all the data. The embedding model, the initial clustering with Mini-batch K-Means, and the representative customer selection are all computationally cheap, especially compared to LLMs. Hence the clustering algorithm can effectively scale to large datasets (38 million samples in our recommendation use case described in Section 5). Section 4.1 shows the speed advantage of the proposed algorithm against various benchmark methods. Section F.3 shows that even with a relatively high minimal similarity requirement of 0.75, we can still achieve 186-fold reduction in data size.

We perform clustering on the embeddings of the customer personas to capture their semantic similarity, a better approach than near-deduplication approaches based on lexical similarity like MinHash (Broder, 1997), as lexical similarity cannot handle paraphrases and does not always align with semantic similarity. SentenceTransformer (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) provides a variety of embedding models and their performance and latency benchmarks to help with model selection. Our first selection criterion is for the output embeddings to support both Euclidean distance (used during initial clustering with Mini-batch K-means) and Cosine similarity (used during representative customer selection). The next criterion is for the embedding model to perform well across multiple benchmark datasets while having a reasonable latency. Based on these criteria, we select "all-MiniLM-L6-v2" as the embedding model for the recommendation use case, but other embedding models that satisfy these criteria can be used as well.

The initial clustering need not be precise, since the subsequent representative selection will further partition it. We thus choose Mini-batch K-Means, which is significantly faster and more memory-efficient than standard K-Means while achieving similar results (Sculley, 2010). The further partition step also makes our algorithm robust to its hyperparameters (Appendix F.4). The number of initial clusters KK, however, controls a meaningful trade-off: increasing KK reduces Stage 2 time linearly and peak memory quadratically (Appendix E), but also slightly reduces data-reduction efficiency by potentially separating similar customers into different initial clusters. On 100K shopping personas, varying KK from 10 to 250 changes the final cluster count by only ∼50%{\sim}50\% while keeping minimal within-cluster similarity at the user-specified threshold (Table 3). In practice we recommend the smallest KK that latency and memory budgets allow.

Appendix D Formal Guarantees of the Proposed Algorithm

In this section we prove that both Algorithm 3.2 (the base two-stage algorithm) and Algorithm C (the optional reassignment variant) satisfy the minimal similarity and attribute matching requirements stated in Section 1 (Requirements 1 and 2). We formalize the argument through the lens of set cover, which naturally captures the representative-selection step.

D.1 Preliminaries and Notation

Let 𝒟={(Pi,Ai)}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(P_{i},A_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} be the input dataset, with embeddings Ei=femb​(Pi)E_{i}=f_{\text{emb}}(P_{i}). For a user-specified similarity threshold α∈[−1,1]\alpha\in[-1,1] and attribute space, define the match relation ∼α\sim_{\alpha} on 𝒟\mathcal{D} by

i∼αj⇔fsim(Ei,Ej)≥α and Ai=Aj.i\sim_{\alpha}j\;\iff\;f_{\text{sim}}(E_{i},E_{j})\geq\alpha\;\text{ and }\;A_{i}=A_{j}.

For any i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, let the α\alpha-ball (or admissible set) of ii be

ℬα(i)={j∈{1,…,n}:i∼αj}.\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i)\;=\;\{\,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}:i\sim_{\alpha}j\,\}.

Note that ∼α\sim_{\alpha} is reflexive (since fsim​(Ei,Ei)=1≥αf_{\text{sim}}(E_{i},E_{i})=1\geq\alpha for any reasonable α≤1\alpha\leq 1, and trivially Ai=AiA_{i}=A_{i}) and symmetric (since fsimf_{\text{sim}} is symmetric and equality of attributes is symmetric), so i∈ℬα​(i)i\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i) and j∈ℬα​(i)⇔i∈ℬα​(j)j\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i)\iff i\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(j). It is not transitive in general, which is why clustering under this relation is non-trivial.

A cluster assignment f^cluster:𝒟→{1,…,n}\hat{f}_{\text{cluster}}:\mathcal{D}\to\{1,\dots,n\} with representative set ℛ⊆{1,…,n}\mathcal{R}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\} is said to satisfy the guardrail property if

f^cluster​(Pi,Ai)=r⟹r∈ℛ​ and ​i∈ℬα​(r).\hat{f}_{\text{cluster}}(P_{i},A_{i})=r\;\Longrightarrow\;r\in\mathcal{R}\;\text{ and }\;i\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(r). (2)

Equivalently, (2) says that every customer is assigned to a representative whose α\alpha-ball covers them. This is precisely the condition required by Requirements 1 and 2.

D.2 Set-Cover Interpretation

Within any initial cluster Ck⊆{1,…,n}C_{k}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\} produced in Stage 1, consider the collection of candidate cover sets

ℱk={ℬα​(i)∩Ck:i∈Ck}.\mathcal{F}_{k}\;=\;\bigl\{\,\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i)\cap C_{k}\;:\;i\in C_{k}\,\bigr\}.

Stage 2 of Algorithm 3.2 is exactly the classical greedy algorithm for Set Cover applied to the universe CkC_{k} with candidate sets ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}: at each iteration it picks the set covering the largest number of still-uncovered elements, removes those elements, and repeats until the universe is exhausted. Because ∼α\sim_{\alpha} is reflexive, every element i∈Cki\in C_{k} is contained in at least one candidate set (namely ℬα​(i)∩Ck\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i)\cap C_{k}), so a valid cover always exists and the greedy procedure terminates.

D.3 Correctness of Algorithm 3.2

Theorem 1 (Guardrail guarantee for Algorithm 3.2).

For any input 𝒟\mathcal{D}, any embedding function fembf_{\text{emb}}, any symmetric similarity function fsimf_{\text{sim}} with fsim​(x,x)≥αf_{\text{sim}}(x,x)\geq\alpha, any threshold α\alpha, and any number of initial clusters K≥1K\geq 1, the assignment f^cluster\hat{f}_{\text{cluster}} returned by Algorithm 3.2 satisfies the guardrail property (2). In particular, for every i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, letting r=f^cluster​(Pi,Ai)r=\hat{f}_{\text{cluster}}(P_{i},A_{i}),

fsim​(femb​(Pi),femb​(Pr))≥αandAi=Ar.f_{\text{sim}}\!\bigl(f_{\text{emb}}(P_{i}),f_{\text{emb}}(P_{r})\bigr)\;\geq\;\alpha\qquad\text{and}\qquad A_{i}=A_{r}.
Proof.

Fix an initial cluster CkC_{k} produced in Stage 1, and consider Stage 2 applied to CkC_{k}. Let 𝒰(t)\mathcal{U}^{(t)} denote the set of unmatched customers at the start of iteration tt, with 𝒰(1)=Ck\mathcal{U}^{(1)}=C_{k}.

At iteration tt, the algorithm computes, for each i∈Cki\in C_{k},

ℳi(t)={j∈𝒰(t):Mi​j=1}=ℬα​(i)∩𝒰(t),\mathcal{M}_{i}^{(t)}\;=\;\{\,j\in\mathcal{U}^{(t)}\,:\,M_{ij}=1\,\}\;=\;\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i)\cap\mathcal{U}^{(t)},

where the second equality follows from the definition Mi​j=𝟏{Si​j≥α and Ai=Aj}M_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{S_{ij}\geq\alpha\text{ and }A_{i}=A_{j}\} in line 7 of Algorithm 3.2. It then selects r∗(t)=arg⁡maxi∈Ck​|ℳi(t)|r^{*(t)}=\arg\max_{i\in C_{k}}|\mathcal{M}_{i}^{(t)}| and assigns every j∈ℳr∗(t)(t)j\in\mathcal{M}_{r^{*(t)}}^{(t)} to representative r∗(t)r^{*(t)} (line 14). By construction,

j∈ℳr∗(t)(t)⟹j∈ℬα​(r∗(t)),j\in\mathcal{M}_{r^{*(t)}}^{(t)}\;\Longrightarrow\;j\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(r^{*(t)}),

so fsim​(Ej,Er∗(t))≥αf_{\text{sim}}(E_{j},E_{r^{*(t)}})\geq\alpha and Aj=Ar∗(t)A_{j}=A_{r^{*(t)}}. The set ℳr∗(t)(t)\mathcal{M}_{r^{*(t)}}^{(t)} is then removed from 𝒰(t+1)\mathcal{U}^{(t+1)} (line 15), so no customer is ever reassigned within Stage 2, and every customer assigned in iteration tt satisfies (2).

Since ∼α\sim_{\alpha} is reflexive, r∗(t)∈ℳr∗(t)(t)r^{*(t)}\in\mathcal{M}_{r^{*(t)}}^{(t)}, so at least one element is removed per iteration, guaranteeing termination in at most |Ck||C_{k}| iterations with 𝒰(T+1)=∅\mathcal{U}^{(T+1)}=\emptyset. Hence every i∈Cki\in C_{k} is assigned to some representative r∈Ckr\in C_{k} with i∈ℬα​(r)i\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(r). Because Stage 1 partitions {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} into {Ck}k=1K\{C_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} and Stage 2 is applied independently within each CkC_{k}, the guarantee extends to every i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}. ∎

Corollary 2 (Cover interpretation).

Let ℛk⊆Ck\mathcal{R}_{k}\subseteq C_{k} be the representatives selected by Stage 2 within initial cluster CkC_{k}. Then {ℬα​(r)∩Ck}r∈ℛk\{\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(r)\cap C_{k}\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{k}} is a valid cover of CkC_{k}, and ℛ=⋃k=1Kℛk\mathcal{R}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{R}_{k} induces the final cluster assignment. The final number of clusters is exactly |ℛ|=∑k=1K|ℛk||\mathcal{R}|=\sum_{k=1}^{K}|\mathcal{R}_{k}|.

Remark 3 (Role of the initial clustering).

Theorem 1 holds for any partition {Ck}k=1K\{C_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} used in Stage 1, including the trivial partition K=1K=1. The choice of initial clustering affects only the number of final clusters and the runtime/memory (Appendix B in the main paper), not the correctness of the guardrails. This is consistent with the empirical robustness reported in Table 3.

D.4 Correctness of Algorithm C (Reassignment Variant)

Theorem 4 (Guardrail guarantee for Algorithm C).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1, the assignment f^cluster\hat{f}_{\text{cluster}} returned after applying Algorithm C to the output of Algorithm 3.2 also satisfies the guardrail property (2). Moreover, for every customer ii, the post-reassignment similarity is at least as large as the original:

fsim​(Ei,Ef^clusternew​(Pi,Ai))≥fsim​(Ei,Ef^clusterold​(Pi,Ai)).f_{\text{sim}}\!\left(E_{i},\,E_{\hat{f}_{\mathrm{cluster}}^{\mathrm{new}}(P_{i},A_{i})}\right)\;\geq\;f_{\text{sim}}\!\left(E_{i},\,E_{\hat{f}_{\mathrm{cluster}}^{\mathrm{old}}(P_{i},A_{i})}\right).

where f^clusterold\hat{f}_{\text{cluster}}^{\mathrm{old}} and f^clusternew\hat{f}_{\text{cluster}}^{\mathrm{new}} denote the assignments before and after reassignment, respectively.

Proof.

Fix an initial cluster CkC_{k} and let ℛk⊆Ck\mathcal{R}_{k}\subseteq C_{k} be the representatives produced by Algorithm 3.2. For each i∈Cki\in C_{k}, Algorithm C (line 2) defines

r∗\displaystyle r^{*} =argmaxr∈ℛk:Mi​r=1Si​r\displaystyle=\;\mathrm{argmax}_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{k}\,:\,M_{ir}=1}S_{ir}
=argmaxr∈ℛk∩ℬα​(i)​fsim​(Ei,Er).\displaystyle=\;\mathrm{argmax}_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{k}\,\cap\,\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i)}f_{\text{sim}}(E_{i},E_{r}).

The reassignment is performed only if the constraint set ℛk∩ℬα​(i)\mathcal{R}_{k}\cap\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i) is nonempty (line 3), in which case r∗∈ℬα​(i)r^{*}\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i) by definition, so the guardrail property (2) is preserved.

If ℛk∩ℬα​(i)\mathcal{R}_{k}\cap\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i) is empty, the assignment is left unchanged; by Theorem 1 the original assignment already satisfied the guardrail, so it still does.

However, by Theorem 1 the original representative rold=f^clusterold​(Pi,Ai)r^{\mathrm{old}}=\hat{f}_{\text{cluster}}^{\mathrm{old}}(P_{i},A_{i}) belongs to ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k} and satisfies i∈ℬα​(rold)i\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(r^{\mathrm{old}}), equivalently rold∈ℬα​(i)r^{\mathrm{old}}\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i) by symmetry of ∼α\sim_{\alpha}. Hence ℛk∩ℬα​(i)\mathcal{R}_{k}\cap\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}(i) is always nonempty, and the reassignment always executes. Moreover, since roldr^{\mathrm{old}} is a feasible candidate in the arg⁡max\arg\max,

fsim​(Ei,Er∗)≥fsim​(Ei,Erold),f_{\text{sim}}(E_{i},E_{r^{*}})\;\geq\;f_{\text{sim}}(E_{i},E_{r^{\mathrm{old}}}),

establishing the monotonicity claim. ∎

Remark 5 (Representative set is preserved).

Algorithm C does not modify ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k}; it only redistributes the non-representative customers within CkC_{k} among the existing representatives. Therefore the final number of clusters |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| is identical for both variants, while the within-cluster similarities can only weakly increase. This explains the empirical observation in Table 1 that the “Proposed w/ Reassign.” variant achieves higher average similarity at the same minimal similarity α\alpha and the same number of clusters as “Proposed Clustering”.

Remark 6 (Trade-off with tail-cluster trimming).

While reassignment preserves the guardrail and improves average similarity, it redistributes mass from the largest (earliest-selected) clusters to smaller ones, flattening the cluster-size distribution. Tail-cluster trimming (Section 4.2) therefore covers fewer customers per retained cluster under Algorithm C, consistent with Figures 3 and 4.

D.5 Relation to the Minimum Set Cover Problem

The greedy step in Stage 2 is the classical Johnson–Chvátal greedy heuristic for Set Cover. Let OPTk\mathrm{OPT}_{k} denote the minimum number of α\alpha-balls needed to cover CkC_{k}. Then the greedy procedure yields

|ℛk|≤OPTk⋅(1+ln⁡|Ck|),|\mathcal{R}_{k}|\;\leq\;\mathrm{OPT}_{k}\cdot\bigl(1+\ln|C_{k}|\bigr),

so the total number of final clusters satisfies

|ℛ|=∑k=1K|ℛk|≤(1+ln⁡maxk​|Ck|)​∑k=1KOPTk.|\mathcal{R}|\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}|\mathcal{R}_{k}|\;\leq\;\bigl(1+\ln\max_{k}|C_{k}|\bigr)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{OPT}_{k}.

This provides a formal ceiling on the data reduction loss incurred by the greedy representative selection, relative to the (NP-hard) optimum cover within each initial cluster. We emphasize that this bound concerns data-reduction efficiency, not correctness: the guardrail property (2) holds exactly, not approximately.

Remark 7 (Partition-constrained vs. global optimum).

The bound above compares |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| to the optimum ℛpartition∗\mathcal{R}^{*}_{\text{partition}} subject to the Stage 1 partition {Ck}\{C_{k}\}. The unconstrained optimum ℛglobal∗\mathcal{R}^{*}_{\text{global}} (ignoring partition boundaries) can be strictly smaller, since two similar customers split across different CkC_{k} cannot share a representative in our algorithm. The gap |ℛpartition∗|−|ℛglobal∗||\mathcal{R}^{*}_{\text{partition}}|-|\mathcal{R}^{*}_{\text{global}}| is controlled by the quality of the initial clustering; in our setting Mini-batch K-Means is empirically sufficient to keep this gap small (Table 3 in Appendix F.4).

Appendix E Computational Complexity Analysis

We analyze the time and memory complexity of Algorithm 3.2 and Algorithm C as a function of the dataset size nn, the embedding dimension dd, the number of initial clusters KK, and the attribute-vector dimension aa. Let nk=|Ck|n_{k}=|C_{k}| denote the size of the kk-th initial cluster, with ∑k=1Knk=n\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}=n.

E.1 Stage 1: Initial Clustering with Mini-Batch K-Means

Let bb be the Mini-batch K-Means batch size and T1T_{1} the number of iterations. A standard Mini-batch K-Means update evaluates bb points against KK centroids in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and performs bb centroid updates per iteration, yielding

TStage 1=O⁡(T1​b​K​d),MStage 1=O⁡((n+K)​d),T_{\text{Stage 1}}\;=\;O\bigl(T_{1}\,b\,K\,d\bigr),\qquad M_{\text{Stage 1}}\;=\;O\bigl((n+K)\,d\bigr),

where the memory term accounts for storing the nn embeddings and KK centroids. Since bb and T1T_{1} are user-specified constants independent of nn, Stage 1 is effectively linear in nn: O⁡(n​d)O(n\,d) memory and (amortized) O⁡(K​d)O(K\,d) time per mini-batch update. This is consistent with Sculley (2010).

E.2 Stage 2: Pairwise Similarity, Match Matrix, and Greedy Selection

Stage 2 is executed independently within each initial cluster CkC_{k}. Within CkC_{k} we perform the following substeps.

(a) Pairwise similarity matrix.

Computing Si​j=fsim​(Ei,Ej)S_{ij}=f_{\text{sim}}(E_{i},E_{j}) for all i,j∈Cki,j\in C_{k} costs O⁡(nk2​d)O(n_{k}^{2}\,d) time and O⁡(nk2)O(n_{k}^{2}) memory.

(b) Attribute match matrix.

Computing Mi​j=𝟏{Si​j≥α and Ai=Aj}M_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{S_{ij}\geq\alpha\text{ and }A_{i}=A_{j}\} costs O⁡(nk2​a)O(n_{k}^{2}\,a) time and O⁡(nk2)O(n_{k}^{2}) memory (assuming aa-dimensional categorical attributes compared in O⁡(a)O(a)). In practice one can precompute attribute group IDs in O⁡(nk​a)O(n_{k}\,a) and reduce the pairwise attribute check to an O⁡(1)O(1) equality test, giving O⁡(nk2)O(n_{k}^{2}) total.

(c) Iterative greedy representative selection.

Let TkT_{k} be the number of greedy iterations within CkC_{k} (i.e., Tk=|ℛk|T_{k}=|\mathcal{R}_{k}|). In each iteration the algorithm must find r∗=arg⁡maxi∈Ck​|ℳi(t)|,r^{*}=\arg\max_{i\in C_{k}}|\mathcal{M}_{i}^{(t)}|, where ℳi(t)={j∈𝒰(t):Mi​j=1}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{(t)}=\{j\in\mathcal{U}^{(t)}:M_{ij}=1\}. A straightforward implementation maintains a row-sum vector of MM restricted to 𝒰(t)\mathcal{U}^{(t)}:

  • •

    Initialization of row sums: O⁡(nk2)O(n_{k}^{2}).

  • •

    Per iteration: select r∗r^{*} in O⁡(nk)O(n_{k}), then update row sums by subtracting the columns of MM indexed by ℳr∗(t)\mathcal{M}_{r^{*}}^{(t)}, costing O⁡(|ℳr∗(t)|⋅nk)O(|\mathcal{M}_{r^{*}}^{(t)}|\cdot n_{k}).

Since the sets ℳr∗(t)(t)\mathcal{M}_{r^{*(t)}}^{(t)} partition CkC_{k}, ∑t|ℳr∗(t)(t)|=nk\sum_{t}|\mathcal{M}_{r^{*(t)}}^{(t)}|=n_{k}, and the total cost of all updates across all TkT_{k} iterations is O⁡(nk2)O(n_{k}^{2}). Hence the greedy loop runs in O⁡(nk2)O(n_{k}^{2}) time.

Per-cluster Stage 2 complexity.

Combining (a)–(c):

TStage 2​(Ck)\displaystyle T_{\text{Stage 2}}(C_{k}) =O⁡(nk2​d+nk2)=O⁡(nk2​d),\displaystyle\;=\;O\bigl(n_{k}^{2}\,d+n_{k}^{2}\bigr)\;=\;O(n_{k}^{2}\,d),
MStage 2​(Ck)\displaystyle M_{\text{Stage 2}}(C_{k}) =O⁡(nk2).\displaystyle\;=\;O(n_{k}^{2}).

Aggregate Stage 2 complexity.

Summing over initial clusters,

TStage 2=O⁡(d​∑k=1Knk2),MStage 2=O⁡(maxk⁡nk2),T_{\text{Stage 2}}\;=\;O\!\left(d\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}^{2}\right),\quad M_{\text{Stage 2}}\;=\;O\!\left(\max_{k}n_{k}^{2}\right),

assuming Stage 2 is processed one initial cluster at a time (so that only one pairwise matrix is held in memory). If initial clusters are roughly balanced with nk≈n/Kn_{k}\approx n/K,

TStage 2=O⁡(n2​dK),MStage 2=O⁡(n2K2).T_{\text{Stage 2}}\;=\;O\!\left(\tfrac{n^{2}d}{K}\right),\qquad M_{\text{Stage 2}}\;=\;O\!\left(\tfrac{n^{2}}{K^{2}}\right).

This formalizes the role of KK: increasing KK decreases Stage 2 time linearly and peak memory quadratically, at the cost of slightly reduced data-reduction efficiency (Appendix F.4, Table 3).

E.3 Stage 2b: Reassignment Step (Algorithm C)

Within initial cluster CkC_{k} with representatives ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k}, the reassignment loop (Algorithm C) examines, for each i∈Cki\in C_{k}, only the columns of SS indexed by ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k}. The cost is O⁡(nk​|ℛk|)O(n_{k}\,|\mathcal{R}_{k}|) per cluster and

TReassign=O⁡(∑k=1Knk​|ℛk|)≤O⁡(∑k=1Knk2),T_{\text{Reassign}}\;=\;O\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}\,|\mathcal{R}_{k}|\right)\;\leq\;O\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}^{2}\right),

which is dominated by the pairwise similarity computation and does not increase the asymptotic complexity. No additional pairwise storage is needed because SS and MM have already been materialized in Stage 2. This matches the empirical observation that the reassignment variant has essentially identical runtime to the base algorithm (Table 1, “Time” column).

E.4 Overall Complexity

Combining Stage 1 and Stage 2,

Ttotal\displaystyle T_{\text{total}} =O⁡(T1​b​K​d+d​∑k=1Knk2),\displaystyle\;=\;O\!\left(T_{1}\,b\,K\,d\;+\;d\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}^{2}\right),
Mtotal\displaystyle M_{\text{total}} =O⁡(n​d+maxk⁡nk2).\displaystyle\;=\;O\!\left(n\,d\;+\;\max_{k}n_{k}^{2}\right).

For roughly balanced initial clusters with nk≈n/Kn_{k}\approx n/K,

Ttotal=O⁡(n​d+n2​dK),Mtotal=O⁡(n​d+n2K2).T_{\text{total}}\;=\;O\!\left(nd+\tfrac{n^{2}d}{K}\right),\qquad M_{\text{total}}\;=\;O\!\left(nd+\tfrac{n^{2}}{K^{2}}\right).

In the regime K=Θ⁡(n)K=\Theta(n) (i.e., nk=O⁡(1)n_{k}=O(1)), Stage 2 becomes O⁡(n​d)O(n\,d), matching Stage 1, and the overall algorithm is linear in nn.

E.5 Comparison with Baselines

For reference, the baseline methods compared in Section 4.1 have the following standard complexities on nn points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}:

  • •

    K-Means (Lloyd): O⁡(n​K​d​T)O(nKdT) time, O⁡(n​d)O(nd) memory.

  • •

    Mini-batch K-Means: O⁡(b​K​d​T)O(bKdT) time, O⁡(n​d)O(nd) memory.

  • •

    Agglomerative (Ward): O⁡(n2​d)O(n^{2}d) time, O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) memory (storing the full distance matrix or heap).

  • •

    BIRCH: O⁡(n​d)O(nd) amortized time, but with large constants.

  • •

    Spectral Clustering: O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) time in the dense case, with O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) memory for the affinity matrix.

  • •

    Gaussian Mixture (EM): O⁡(n​K​d2​T)O(nKd^{2}T) time, O⁡(n​d+K​d2)O(nd+Kd^{2}) memory.

None of these baselines admit a user-specified minimal within-cluster similarity constraint, and the O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) memory requirement of Agglomerative and Spectral clustering is prohibitive at the n=38n=38M scale (as noted in Section 4: ∼90\sim 90 TB for n=5n=5M). Algorithm 3.2 circumvents this by restricting the quadratic computation to within each initial cluster, yielding O⁡(maxk⁡nk2)≪O⁡(n2)O(\max_{k}n_{k}^{2})\ll O(n^{2}) memory for any K≫1K\gg 1. This is the underlying reason for the 10×10\times–1000×1000\times runtime advantage observed in Table 1.

Appendix F Additional Experiment Results

F.1 Cluster Size Distributions

As detailed in Section 3, the iterative greedy selection of representative samples in the proposed algorithm by design leads to highly skewed cluster size distribution, with practical advantages: We can remove a large percentage of tail clusters at the cost of removing a small percentage of samples, improving data size reduction; in the case of personalized recommendation, if quality assurance is expensive, we can focus on the top clusters by size. We examine how many overall samples the top clusters by size can cover for different clustering methods in Figure 3 and Figure 4 based on the experiment output from Section 4.1.

We see that as the percentage of top clusters increases, the proposed clustering algorithm can cover significantly more samples than other clustering methods. The practical implication, for example, is that we can keep only 4% of clusters to cover 90% of customers when generating personalized recommendations for a further 25-fold reduction in downstream computation cost and latency. The customer removal can be compensated for by oversampling customers in the beginning.

F.2 Relevance Rating v.s. Similarity Figure

We show the scatterplot of relevance rating vs the member-representative similarity in Figure 5, empirically validating using the minimal within-cluster similarity as quality guardrails of product recommendations.

F.3 Impact of Minimal Similarity and Household Attributes

There is a trade-off between within-cluster similarity and the number of clusters. In the case of personalized recommendations, the higher the similarity, the more likely we recommend the relevant products to all customers in a cluster, at the cost of increasing the number of clusters and thus downstream computations. Similarly, the number of clusters will increase if we require matching household attributes in addition to the persona similarity, such as adult gender, adult count, child presence, child gender, and child age. These household attributes are important for personalized recommendations and not always captured in the customer shopping personas. We show how the number of clusters is affected by the minimal similarity and matching attributes required between each sample and the cluster representative in Table 2 on randomly selected 5 million customers of the 38 million customer dataset.

F.4 Impact of Hyperparameters and Robustness

We perform the proposed clustering with reassignment step on the 100K Shopping Personas for different hyperparameters of Mini-batch K-Means used for the initial clustering before representative selection. Because the greedy selection and optional reassignment in the second stage help further partition the initial clusters based on desired safety/quality constraints, the proposed clustering method is robust to the hyperparameters of Mini-batch K-Means or even the choice of the clustering method used in the first stage (Table 3).

There are two main tradeoffs in our clustering application. The first main tradeoff is between cluster quality and data reduction fold, which impacts the recommendation quality and downstream computation savings. This tradeoff is controlled by the user specified minimal similarity threshold and matching attributes shown in Table 2. The second main tradeoff is between scalability (in terms of latency and memory usage) and data reduction fold. This tradeoff is controlled by the initial number of clusters, KK. Recall that in the second stage of the proposed clustering we compute pairwise embedding similarity within each initial cluster for the greedy representative selection. This pairwise computation is O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) w.r.t. sample size nn, in this case the size of each initial cluster. Thus as KK increases, the latency and memory requirement will both decrease, increasing scalability. In exchange, the initial clustering also introduces noise so that samples that pass the final cluster criteria might end up separated during initial clustering, reducing the efficiency of data size reduction, which worsens as KK increases (Table 3). In practice we recommend choosing a KK as small as latency and memory requirements allow to maximize data reduction.

Appendix G Experimental Setup Details

In the experiment on within-cluster similarities from Section 4.1, we specify the minimal similarity thresholds (0.75 on internal shopping personas, 0.3 on AG News, and 0.4 on Cosmopedia) to obtain ∼\sim50 fold reduction in data size based on our target use case in personalized recommendation and for making results across 3 datasets more comparable. The conclusions are consistent for other values of minimal similarity thresholds based on further experiments. We set the number of initial clusters to be 0.04% of the sample size. Increasing this ratio will reduce the memory requirement of pair-wise similarity computation within each initial cluster at the potential cost of increasing the number of final clusters.

We use the default hyperparameters of the clustering methods benchmarked against as implemented in Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) 1.7.2, except for Spectral Clustering whose hyperparameters are slightly adjusted for memory efficiency. The number of clusters is set to match the final number of clusters produced by the proposed clustering algorithm on each dataset to achieve the same data size reduction. Other key hyperparameters are as follows:

  1. 1.

    Mini-batch K-Means: ‘max_iter’: 100, ‘batch_size’: 10240, ‘init_size’: 30720, ‘random_state’: 123.

  2. 2.

    K-Means: ‘init’: ‘k-means++’, ‘n_init’: ‘auto’, ‘max_iter’: 300, ‘algorithm’: ‘lloyd’.

  3. 3.

    Agglomerative Clustering: ‘metric’: ‘euclidean’, ‘linkage’: ‘ward’, ‘compute_full_tree’: ‘auto’.

  4. 4.

    BIRCH: ‘threshold’: 0.5, ‘branching_factor’: 50.

  5. 5.

    Spectral Clustering: ‘affinity’: ‘nearest_neighbors’, ‘n_neighbors’: 10, ‘eigen_solver’: ‘lobpcg’.

  6. 6.

    Gaussian Mixture: ‘covariance_type’: ‘full’, ‘init_params’: ‘kmeans’, ‘max_iter’: 100.
